name: Rocket Science & Spaceflight
tagline: Design, analyse and fly rockets and spacecraft.
description: For anyone who wants to go from watching launches to understanding and designing them. You start with the maths and a model rocket, build up the mechanical, thermal-fluid and aerodynamic engineering, then learn propulsion, orbital mechanics, launch and re-entry, guidance and control, avionics and flight software, and finish by designing a complete space mission.
outcomes: Size a multi-stage launch vehicle with the rocket equation and estimate its payload to orbit
Analyse a liquid, solid or hybrid rocket engine: propellant performance, nozzle expansion, cooling and feed system
Plan orbits, transfers and interplanetary trajectories, and build a delta-v budget for a mission
Estimate entry heating and choose a thermal protection and landing approach for a returning vehicle
Design attitude determination and control and a Kalman-filter navigation loop for a spacecraft
Write and structure real-time flight software for an embedded flight computer
Carry a spacecraft from mission requirements through subsystem trades to an integrated, testable design

stages.name: Mathematical foundations
stages.description: The algebra, geometry, trigonometry and basic statistics that every flight calculation is built on.

items.why: Ratios, powers and scientific notation are needed for mass ratios, thrust-to-weight and unit conversions.
Rearranging the rocket equation and performance formulas is everyday algebra.
Geometry of nozzles, fins, tanks and trajectories starts with Euclid.
Resolving thrust, drag and gravity into components along a flight path is trigonometry.
Exponentials and logarithms: the rocket equation is a logarithm of the mass ratio.
Orbits are conic sections; you will use ellipse and hyperbola geometry constantly.
Summarising test data, from motor burns to sensor logs, starts with means, spread and plots.
Reliability, dispersion and risk in launch are all probability.

stages.name: Hands-on start: how rockets fly
stages.description: Build intuition and fly something: the physics of rockets and orbits at a conceptual level, plus model rocketry.

items.why: Units and vectors: mixing up units has destroyed real spacecraft, and forces and velocities are vectors.
Newton's laws, momentum and gravity are exactly why and how a rocket works.
A map of the field: vehicles, disciplines and the units aerospace engineers use.
Action and reaction, thrust, specific impulse and staging explained before the equations arrive.
The hands-on start: build and fly model and high-power rockets safely, and learn stability, recovery and motor choice by doing.
What orbit means, why it takes about 7.8 km/s, and the main orbit types, before the formal mechanics.
Lift, drag and speed regimes; rockets fly through the same atmosphere as aircraft.

stages.name: Calculus, statistics & computing
stages.description: The engineering mathematics and programming used in every later analysis.

items.why: Thrust, mass flow and trajectories are rates of change; the rocket equation itself comes from an integral.
Rotation matrices, state vectors and Kalman filters are linear algebra.
Flow fields, heat flux and structural stress vary in three dimensions.
Equations of motion for rockets, orbits and control loops are ODEs.
Conservation laws in fluid mechanics and heat transfer are written with divergence and gradient.
Laplace transforms turn control-system dynamics into algebra; Fourier transforms analyse vibration and signals.
Random variables and covariance are the basis of navigation filters, dispersions and reliability.
Confidence intervals and tests tell you whether a test-stand result is real.
Fourier series, separation of variables and Bessel functions solve heat, vibration and acoustic problems.
Heat conduction, wave propagation and fluid flow are PDEs; you need the classical equations and characteristics.
A quick grounding in how computers represent data before you start programming.
Python is the everyday tool for trajectory simulation, data reduction and design scripts.
Numerical integration, root finding and linear solvers applied to aerospace problems such as trajectory propagation.

stages.name: Physics, chemistry & circuits
stages.description: Classical physics, the chemistry behind combustion and the electrical basics every flight system needs.

items.why: Heat, temperature and gas laws come before engine thermodynamics.
Charges, fields and circuits, the base for avionics, power systems and electric propulsion.
Central forces, rotating frames and rigid-body motion are the physics of orbits and attitude.
3D rigid-body dynamics in rotating frames: the mechanical basis of flight mechanics, orbits and attitude.
Fields, induction and EM waves are needed for electric thrusters, antennas and the space environment.
Voltage, current and power, and working safely with batteries and igniters.
Circuit analysis is needed for instrumentation, power systems and avionics.
Moles, reactions and stoichiometry: every propellant calculation starts here.
Atomic structure explains why hydrogen, oxygen and certain metals make good propellants and structures.
Bond energies are where propellant energy is stored.
Gases, liquids and phase behaviour matter for cryogenic propellants and tank pressurisation.
Heats of formation and reaction set how much energy a propellant combination releases.
Reaction rates decide ignition, burn rate and whether combustion is stable.
Equilibrium and dissociation at chamber temperatures set exhaust composition and performance.

stages.name: Mechanics, structures, materials & control
stages.description: Mechanical-engineering fundamentals: how structures carry load, what they are made of, how they vibrate and how feedback control works.

items.why: The engineering design process and habits used throughout vehicle design.
Free-body diagrams and equilibrium: loads on a rocket on the pad and in flight.
Engineering dynamics of particles and rigid bodies, the base for vibration and flight mechanics.
Stress, strain, bending and buckling size tanks, interstages and thrust structures.
Why metals, ceramics, polymers and composites behave differently.
Properties of engineering alloys and composites as a designer uses them.
Aluminium-lithium, titanium, nickel superalloys and composites: how aerospace materials are chosen.
Thin-walled, stiffened structures are what rockets and spacecraft are made of.
Composite overwrapped tanks, fairings and interstages are laminated structures.
Modelling mechanical, electrical and fluid systems as differential equations and transfer functions.
Rockets shake: modes, damping and forced response.
Launch vibration, acoustic and shock environments and how structures respond.
Classical and state-space control, the foundation for thrust vectoring, attitude and guidance loops.

stages.name: Thermodynamics, fluids & aerodynamics
stages.description: Energy, flow and heat: the physics inside engines and around vehicles flying through the atmosphere.

items.why: Energy balances, entropy and cycles, the foundation of propulsion analysis.
Gas mixtures, combustion and cycles; turbopump drive cycles are thermodynamic cycles.
Thermodynamics aimed at propulsion: gas properties, enthalpy and propulsion cycles.
Pressure, flow in pipes and control-volume analysis for feed systems and aerodynamics.
Conduction, convection and radiation size engine cooling, heat shields and spacecraft thermal control.
Navier-Stokes, boundary layers, compressible flow and cavitation for engine and pump design.
Forces, moments and dimensionless numbers for vehicles moving through air.
Potential flow, circulation and lift: the basis of fin and body aerodynamics.
Shocks, expansions and isentropic nozzle flow: the physics of every rocket nozzle and supersonic ascent.
Skin friction, heat transfer and separation, needed for drag, nozzle and entry heating.
Missile and launcher aerodynamics: drag build-up, fin design, centre of pressure and base drag.
Above Mach 5 heating and gas chemistry dominate: essential for re-entry and ascent heating.

stages.name: Rocket propulsion
stages.description: From the rocket equation to real engines: propellants and combustion, nozzles, liquid, solid, hybrid and electric propulsion, and testing.

items.why: The rocket equation, thrust, specific impulse and ideal rocket theory: the core of the whole roadmap.
Gibbs energy and chemical equilibrium are how propellant performance codes compute chamber composition.
Chain reactions and rate theory explain ignition, flame holding and explosions.
Flames, sprays and detonations as they happen inside engines.
Adiabatic flame temperature, dissociation and combustion in rocket chambers.
The chemistry of oxidisers, fuels, monopropellants and solid propellants, and why each is chosen.
How propellant choice sets characteristic velocity and specific impulse; equilibrium performance calculations.
Real nozzle design, expansion ratio, altitude losses and how rockets steer their thrust.
Grain geometry, burn rate and motor design: the scaled-up version of your model rocket motor.
Solid fuel with liquid oxidiser: popular in amateur and university rocketry for safety and throttling.
Thrust chambers, injectors, regenerative cooling and ignition of liquid engines.
Pumps and turbines, velocity triangles and cavitation, the basis of turbopump design.
Pressure-fed versus gas-generator, staged-combustion and expander cycles, turbopumps and tank pressurisation.
Pressure, temperature, force and strain measurement and data acquisition for tests and flight.
Test stands, instrumentation and test safety: how engines are actually proven.
Ion, Hall and other electric thrusters that move spacecraft once they are in space.

stages.name: Orbits, launch vehicles & re-entry
stages.description: Astrodynamics, getting from the pad to orbit, and coming back through the atmosphere.

items.why: The two-body problem, orbital elements and time of flight: the geometry of spaceflight.
Hohmann transfers, plane changes and phasing, and how to build a delta-v budget.
Oblateness, drag, solar pressure and third bodies, and numerical orbit propagation.
Patched conics, launch windows, porkchop plots and gravity assists for the Moon and planets.
Gravity turns, gravity and drag losses and ascent simulation from pad to orbit.
Staging, propulsion selection, structures and mass budgets brought together into a launch vehicle.
Controlling a flexible, sloshing, aerodynamically unstable rocket and the loads that result.
Ballistic and lifting entry, deceleration, heating and entry corridors.
Ablative and reusable heat shields: materials, sizing and testing.
Parachutes, inflatable decelerators, retropropulsion and precision landing.
Propulsive landing, recovery and refurbishment, and the economics of reuse.

stages.name: Guidance, navigation & control
stages.description: Knowing where the vehicle is, deciding where it should go and steering it there, for rockets and spacecraft.

items.why: Least squares and Kalman filters are behind every navigation system.
Quaternions, Euler angles and rigid-body attitude dynamics.
Star trackers, sun sensors, gyros and filters to work out which way the spacecraft points.
Reaction wheels, thrusters and magnetorquers and the control laws that use them.
Inertial, GNSS and deep-space navigation for launchers and spacecraft.
Ascent, transfer, entry and powered-landing guidance laws.
Relative motion, rendezvous and docking, as used for space stations and servicing.
Estimating an orbit from tracking data with batch and sequential filters.
Integrating guidance, navigation and control into a verified flight system with fault management.

stages.name: Avionics, embedded systems & flight software
stages.description: The electronics, embedded computing and software engineering that turn a vehicle into something that can fly itself.

items.why: Breadboarding, soldering and a multimeter: the bench skills for building flight computers and ground-support gear.
Binary numbers and logic gates: how flight computers represent and process data.
Registers, counters and state machines, which also model flight sequencing.
Program a microcontroller to read sensors and fire events: the core of an amateur flight computer.
The shell, scripting and build tools used to develop and test flight code.
Decomposition, testing and debugging discipline for programs bigger than scripts.
Number representation, the processor and interrupts at machine level, which flight software depends on.
C, pointers and memory: most flight software is written in C or C++.
Register-level C, interrupts, timers, ADCs and serial buses on microcontrollers.
Programming without an OS: memory-mapped I/O and interrupt service routines.
Logic, state machines and invariants for reasoning about software correctness.
Queues, buffers and fixed-size structures used in telemetry and command handling.
Scheduling, synchronisation and real-time operating systems.
Critical sections, priority inversion and deadlock: the bugs that have hit real spacecraft.
Deadlines, jitter and worst-case execution time for control loops that must never be late.
Classes and interfaces as used in C++ flight frameworks and ground software.
Version control and code review are mandatory on any flight-software team.
Specifications, testing and defensive programming for code that cannot fail.
Life-cycle, configuration and release management as practised on flight programmes.
Phasors, transforms and discrete-time maths for signals and communications.
Sampling, filtering and transfer functions for sensors, control and radio links.
Sampling, aliasing and digital filtering of sensor and telemetry data.
Accelerometers and gyroscopes: the IMU at the heart of every rocket's navigation.
Digital and robust control as implemented on real flight computers.
Autopilots, inertial and GPS navigation and flight recorders as avionics hardware.

stages.name: Capstone: spacecraft & mission design
stages.description: Spacecraft subsystems, systems engineering and mission design brought together into complete, launchable missions; ends with electives.

items.why: Vacuum, radiation, plasma, atomic oxygen and debris: what every spacecraft must survive.
The spacecraft as a system of subsystems tied together by mass, power and data budgets.
Solar arrays, batteries and power distribution.
Keeping hardware within temperature limits in vacuum with coatings, heaters and radiators.
Antennas, modulation and link budgets: how spacecraft talk to Earth.
The onboard computer, data buses, telemetry and telecommand.
Safety-critical real-time flight software and the lessons of famous software failures.
Structures that survive launch and mechanisms that deploy and point.
Cold-gas, monopropellant and bipropellant in-space propulsion, tanks and feed systems.
Requirements, interfaces, reviews and verification, the NASA way of building complex vehicles.
Redundant avionics architectures, networks and integration into the vehicle.
FMEA, fault trees and probabilistic risk, and lessons from accidents.
Launch sites, propellant loading, countdown, range safety and licensing.
Integration and environmental testing: vibration, thermal-vacuum and EMC before shipping to the launch site.
Capstone: the SMAD process of turning objectives into orbit, spacecraft, ground segment, cost and schedule.
Mission control, flight dynamics operations and anomaly response.
Capstone: take a mission from requirements to a balanced, integrated spacecraft design.
Elective: the combustion-acoustic coupling that can destroy liquid engines, and how it is suppressed.
Elective: CubeSats are the most accessible route to building real flight hardware yourself.
Elective: landers, rovers, aerial vehicles and sample return for the Moon, Mars and beyond.
Elective: fixed points, stability and invariant manifolds, groundwork for three-body orbit design.
Elective: Lagrange points, halo orbits and low-energy transfers used by JWST and lunar missions.
Elective: calculus of variations, groundwork for trajectory optimisation.
Elective: mathematical control theory, groundwork for optimal control.
Elective: Pontryagin's principle and optimal control, groundwork for trajectory optimisation.
Elective: minimum-fuel and minimum-time trajectories for launchers, landers and spacecraft.
